"It really does hurt my heart a little bit because I do believe California is the best state in the country, or one of the best. We have amazing infrastructure. We have an amazing business. We are the fourth-largest economy in the world. And on top of it, we have a lifestyle that no other state can provide. And it's sad to see corporations and multimillionaires and billionaires leave for other states, not because they want to, but because they're looking for fiscally responsible states for themselves."
"There's two things we know certain in life: Death and taxes will always be in existence, and it will always be a conversation. But I do believe that California residents, as well as the government, need to start coming together and there needs to be some fiscally smart decision-making when it comes to tax. Because the last thing we wanna do is lose both our big and small businesses to other states."

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO documents show there really is only one risk with AI
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO documents show there really is only one risk with AI
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Of all the risks Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) lists in 80-ish pages of warnings, amounting to almost a third of its IPO prospectus, there really is only one: not investing.
That's the resounding message in the aftermath of the Claude maker's IPO documents getting leaked .
The clear implied message of a frontier AI lab on the verge of becoming a $2 trillion company is that investors should join in. Sure, Anthropic listed the risks. But did you notice the expected $2 trillion valuation? Do you want to miss out on that? If the risks truly mattered, the projected valuation would be much closer to zero.
Potential investors will be confronted with the extraordinary message that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." That's the company's own words via the prospectus, which was reviewed by Reuters. The risks associated with its AI models include "self-preserving behaviors," attempts to "conceal or ‌manipulate information," and behavior "resembling blackmail."
As Reuters notes, Anthropic's IPO risk factors add up to roughly 80 pages of a 261-page document, twice the number of pages the AI lab uses to describe its actual business. SpaceX, which, lest we forget, straps people and cargo onto a controlled explosion and hurls them through the sky into space, used around 38 pages to outline its risk factors.
The financials are just as fraught. Anthropic lost more than $8 billion on an operating basis in 2025, even as revenue grew twelvefold, according to the documents.
But the stark losses, even paired with the existential risks, only underscore just how valuable Anthropic and its backers believe its technology to be. The frontier AI lab views the coming AI era, Reuters reports, as more transformative than industrialization, electricity, and the internet.
The public sale could value the company at more than $2 trillion, leapfrogging almost every major corporation aside from a handful of tech giants, soaking up capital and interest before OpenAI goes to market, and outrunning public warnings about AI's threats to human civilization.
In this light, the dozens of pages of risks look less like formidable liabilities than endearing flaws. Untold future profits outweigh the biggest hypothetical fears.

articles.title_orig: California poll: Voters back a billionaire tax, but the proposal falls short of majority support
articles.title_zh: California poll: Voters back a billionaire tax, but the proposal falls short of majority support
articles.content_orig:
A plurality of likely California voters support a proposal on the state’s November ballot that would impose a one-time wealth tax on the richest Californians , but the measure is still short of majority support, according to a new NBCUniversal Local/Telemundo Station Group poll released Wednesday.
In the poll, 48% said they would vote “yes” on the proposal, while 38% said they would vote “no.” Another 14% said they were undecided.
The 10-point lead for “yes” is outside the poll’s margin of error, which is plus or minus 4 percentage points for each side’s support level.
The spread was almost identical among Hispanic likely voters, according to a companion survey of California : 50% said they’d vote “yes,” 40% said they’d vote “no,” and 10% said they were undecided. Both surveys were conducted Sept. 21-24.
The so-called billionaire tax — which will appear on the November ballot as “Proposition 40” — would implement a one-time 5% tax on the assets of Californians with net worths exceeding $1.1 billion, and it would require the state to spend 90% of the new revenue on healthcare. The remaining 10% would be split between education and food assistance programs.
In addition to the one-time tax on those worth more than $1.1 billion, the measure, if it is passed, would implement a smaller tax on individuals worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. The taxes would apply retroactively to anyone living in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.
The proposal has divided Democratic leaders in California. Prominent proponents — including Rep. Ro Khanna, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, and Tom Steyer, a billionaire activist who unsuccessfully ran for governor — argue it would help close income inequality gaps and help make up for state budget shortfalls as a result of Medicaid cuts in President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.”
Opponents of the ballot measure, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and the Democratic candidate to succeed him this year, Xavier Becerra, have argued the initiative would drive wealthy investors and tech leaders from the state.
The details of the proposal, which has been led by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, a large California healthcare workers union, have also sparked opposition from many other unions and Democratic groups. Those groups have taken issue with the fact that other progressive policy priorities, like public education and food assistance, would benefit far less than healthcare from the new revenue.
Many Democratic critics have also joined forces with some Republicans, many of whom have long argued that a wealth tax could destabilize California’s revenue streams by causing the ultrarich to flee the state.
But the new poll showed California voters were largely not worried about the prospect of wealthy California residents’ leaving.
A total of 59% of respondents said they were either “not” or “not too” concerned about that potential outcome, while a total of 41% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned about rich people’s leaving the state because of the ballot measure. Among Hispanic voters, 62% said they were either “not” or “not too” concerned, while 38% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned.
Notably, the poll also found California voters almost evenly split over whether they approve or disapprove of the job performance of Newsom, widely seen as a 2028 presidential hopeful.
Forty-five percent of respondents said they approved of his job performance, while 46% said they disapproved. Another 9% said they weren’t sure. Hispanic voters were more positive about Newsom, with 54% approving and 38% disapproving of his performance as governor.
But when it came to how Democrats felt about a possible Newsom 2028 bid, they overwhelmingly said they’d get behind him. Asked whether they’d be inclined to vote for him if he ran to become the Democratic Party’s presidential nominee in 2028, 66% of Democratic respondents said yes, 15% said no, and 19% said they weren’t sure.
Another November ballot measure, Proposition 39, would, if it is passed, require voters to show a government-issued ID when they cast ballots in person, while mail-in voters would have to provide the last four digits of a designated ID used during registration. Among likely voters, 49% said they would support the measure, while 42% said they would vote against it, and 9% said they were undecided.
Asked about Proposition 39, 55% of Hispanic voters said they would vote “yes” in support of it, while 38% said they would vote “no,” and 7% said they were undecided.
California voters strongly said cost of living and the economy were among the most important issues when they were deciding to vote, with 25% saying “cost of living/inflation” was the most important and 23% saying “economy/jobs.” Another 15% said “immigration and enforcement” was the most important, while 11% said healthcare, and 10% said “foreign policy and the Iran War.” No other issue registered at more than 5%.
Amid the focus on economic issues, a plurality of respondents — 42% — said their “personal financial situation” was “the same” as four years earlier. Thirty-six percent said it was “worse” compared with four years earlier, while 22% said it was “better.”
Meanwhile, most respondents (64%) in reliably blue California overwhelmingly said they disapproved of the job President Donald Trump was doing. Another 31% said they approved, and 5% said they weren’t sure.
Asked how much impact they felt the conflict with Iran was having on the U.S. economy, more than two-thirds (67%) of respondents said it was having a “great” deal of impact. Another 16% said it was having “some” impact, while 7% said “not much,” and 8% said “none.”
I cover state legislatures, politics and policy — and how those topics coalesce into and intersect with national political trends. Given what state lawmakers have focused on in recent years, my coverage areas tend to veer into reproductive rights, voting rights and education policy. I was born and raised in Milwaukee, and I try to make my native state proud by covering as many of its fascinating political stories as I can.

articles.title_orig: Patients switching to Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill from shots lose more weight in real-world study
articles.title_zh: Patients switching to Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill from shots lose more weight in real-world study
articles.content_orig:
People who switched from obesity injections to Novo 's new Wegovy pill continued to lose weight after three months, according to an analysis of real-world data the company presented on Wednesday.
Real-world studies evaluate associations and can't determine causality. But the results suggest that the Wegovy pill may improve upon the initial weight loss people experience on blockbuster injections rather than simply maintain it. It also suggests that patients may not need to take weekly shots like Wegovy and Zepbound forever, and can instead opt for more convenient treatments such as Novo's pill.
Novo's analysis used data from Ro's telehealth platform on 194 patients with obesity or who were overweight, around 56% of whom were female. Half started on Novo's Wegovy injection and the rest initially took Eli Lilly 's shot Zepbound.
Patients who switched from an injection to the Wegovy pill and stayed on treatment for three months lost roughly 4% of their weight, or an additional 8.8 pounds, on average. That's based on an average starting weight of around 221 pounds before taking the pill, Novo said.
Of those participants, 2 in 5 achieved 5% or more weight loss three months after switching to the pill. Meanwhile, the share of people with a body mass index at or above 30 decreased by more than 21% three months after switching to oral Wegovy. A BMI of 30 shifts a person from the overweight category into obesity.
"We have the unique benefit that, in the market, the subcutaneous Wegovy can now be interchanged with a tablet of Wegovy, and the patient can expect the same tolerability profile, the same safety profile, and actually a little bit more weight loss, which is what a lot of them want," Martin Holst Lange, Novo's chief scientific officer, said in an interview.
Among patients with available data, around 82% reported at least one improvement during treatment with the pill. That includes almost 70% who reported better-fitting clothes and around 51% who said they pursued healthier eating.
Around 75% of patients in the analysis said they were satisfied with the switch to a pill, according to Novo.
"I think we are seeing a shift where we, maybe just a year ago, we actually thought that the vast majority of patients who wanted treatment for obesity were happy with a subcutaneous treatment," Lange said. "We see that picture differently now. We clearly see a preference for orals."
He pointed to people who travel a lot and don't want to think about refrigerating their injections.
It is among the first real-world evidence of weight loss outcomes among patients switching from blockbuster injections, particularly Novo's Wegovy shot and Lilly's rival Zepbound, to the new pill. But the study's limitations include variable timing and completeness of the data collected during routine telehealth care, self-reported data being subject to bias and results "not being generalizable to the broader population," Novo said.
In partnership with Novo, Ro said it's focused on learning from real-world data on its patients that can be used by other stakeholders in the healthcare industry.
"The future of healthcare is personal, and you can't get there without the data," said Zachariah Reitano, Ro co-founder and CEO. "Medicine is very good at answering 'does this work on average.' It's terrible at answering 'what works for you.' That's the gap we can bridge."
"We obsess over what enables patients and providers to achieve the best outcomes for every patient," he added. "Why do some patients respond better than others? What is the optimal titration schedule for each patient? What are the best long term maintenance techniques?"
The figures are also one of several new datasets Novo is unveiling this week on its obesity and diabetes pipeline at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy.
Also on Wednesday, Novo announced that its experimental next-generation obesity drug CagriSema reduced "food noise" — persistent thoughts about food — and showed benefits in organ and bone health. That's based on results from a yearlong functional magnetic resonance imaging study, which is a noninvasive method to measure brain activity during specific tasks.
CagriSema is a combination of Novo's semaglutide — the active ingredient in Wegovy — and a drug called cagrilintide that targets amylin. CagriSema is expected to launch early next year, followed by standalone cagrilintide and a higher-dose version of CagriSema in 2028.
In the study, Novo said CagriSema changed how the brain reacted to tempting, high-calorie foods in areas linked to cravings, pleasure and self-control in people with obesity or who were overweight.
"The signal in the brain changes in a way that actually is associated with improved quality of life," said Lange.
The company added that CagriSema reduced harmful fat around abdominal organs, including in the liver and pancreas, in adults with Type 2 diabetes. Early findings also suggest that patients' bone health was maintained despite substantial weight loss, Novo noted.
The drugmaker said the findings suggest CagriSema may address underlying factors of obesity and diabetes in the brain and multiple organs and tissues, rather than only impacting weight and blood sugar levels.

articles.title_orig: South Korea break China hearts to reach Asian Games football final
articles.title_zh: South Korea break China hearts to reach Asian Games football final
articles.content_orig:
Hosts Japan will play reigning champions South Korea for Asian Games men's football gold after winning a nail-biting semi-final 9-8 on penalties against Uzbekistan on Wednesday.
Japan were heading out before Sena Ishibashi pounced with two minutes left of normal time to make it 1-1 and force extra time.
Uzbekistan, who had taken the lead after only eight minutes through Sardorbek Bakhromov, hung on through the extra period to take the contest to penalties.
But Japan held their nerve to win it from the spot, sparking gleeful celebrations and leaving some of the young Uzbek players in tears.
Asian Games men's football consists of under-23 squads with three overage players.
In the first semi-final, South Korea scored with eight minutes left to seal a 2-1 win over China .
The Koreans are pursuing a fourth title in a row.
Bae Jun-ho was their hero, ghosting in at the back post to head in a dramatic 82nd-minute winner at Nagai Stadium.
"We were expecting a challenging match, but we persevered," said South Korea coach Lee Min-sung.
"We conceded first to make it even harder, but our team fought back, and I'm happy with that."
Lee's side are attempting to bring some cheer to South Korean football fans after a disappointing World Cup that saw the senior team exit in the group stage.
China's men have never won Asian Games football gold and were contesting their first semi-final since 1998.
History looked on the cards when Wang Yudong finished off a smart team move with an emphatic finish to put China ahead on 22 minutes.
In an entertaining encounter in front of a sparse crowd, Lee Young-jun hit back for South Korea 11 minutes later with China goalkeeper Li Hao getting a hand to his header but unable to keep the ball out.
Both sides had chances in the second half, before Stoke City's Bae popped up with the winner.
China coach Antonio Puche will now have to rally his men with a bronze medal on the line against Uzbekistan.
"I spoke with the players and what I said is that even though we lost, the important thing was that we fought," he said.
"We lost, but we are proud."
North Korea will face Japan in the women's final on Friday, with the men's decider on Saturday.

articles.title_zh: Democratic lawmakers call for protections over third country deportations after ‘indefensible’ court ruling – US politics live
articles.content_orig:
Lawmakers say ‘Congress must step in’ after supreme court ruled to allow Trump officials to resume deporting people where their lives could be in danger
US supreme court allows Trump officials to resume deportations to third countries
Sign up for the Breaking News US email
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Democratic lawmakers have called for more formalized steps to prevent the US government from deporting people to countries where their lives would be in danger or they could be subject to torture.
It comes as the US supreme court on Tuesday lifted restrictions on the deportations of immigrants to countries that are not their own, while agreeing to hear the issue on its merits in December.
Rob Menendez, a congressional Democrat, called the supreme court’s decision “indefensible”, adding:
double quotation mark Taxpayers shouldn’t fund tearing people from the only home they’ve ever known, nor should our legal system fast-track these unilateral deportations.
The conservative-dominated high court granted an emergency request by the Trump administration to suspend a lower court ruling that restricted, but did not outright ban, so-called “third-country removals”.
After the ruling, Democratic lawmakers pushed for the tightening of protections to prevent such deportations where lives could be at risk and to uphold due process.
“Congress must step in. No one should be shipped off to a country that is not their own without basic due process and a meaningful opportunity to raise legitimate fears for their safety,” House Democrat Lois Frankel said on X.
The Trump administration has defended third-country deportations as necessary since the home nations of some of those who are targeted for removal sometimes refuse to accept them.
Donald Trump announced that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed on to a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. Trump did not give further details on the controls, but he suggested that the deal would allow the companies to largely “self-police” their products and technology. Later, Trump signed an executive order calling for “artificial intelligence” to be renamed “super intelligence”.
Jack Smith faced Senate lawmakers on the judiciary committee for a contentious hearing that saw a number of Republicans accuse the former special prosecutor of perjury , and conducting a political witch-hunt against Trump when he secured two indictments against the president that were later dismissed when he took office.
A Republican senator blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress. Mike Lee, of Utah, objected when the Oregon Democrat Jeff Merkley asked the Senate to pass the Protecting Presidential Memorials Act by unanimous consent.
The US Senate rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank , including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years.
JD Vance and health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr spoke at the conclusion of the Make America Healthy Again summit in Washington. Several reporters were denied entry to the event.
Federal prosecutors have charged a Venezuelan delivery driver shot by ICE agents in Texas this month with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was shot by federal immigration officers after a traffic stop in Texas on 20 September. The charge echoes similar claims federal immigration officers have made about immigrants and anti-ICE protesters, including Minnesota mother Renee Good, “weaponizing their vehicles”.
On Capitol Hill today, we’ll be keeping an eye on the Senate’s final week in Washington before they leave for the midterm recess.
Top of lawmakers’ agenda today is legislation that would allow states and utilities to consider standards to ensure tech companies foot the bill for the additional energy costs associated with power-intensive datacenters throughout the US .
The bill, known as the Ratepayer Protection act , is seen as political cover for senators running in battlegrounds in the upcoming midterm cycle, where datacenter construction is a huge concern for voters.
Introduced by Republican senator John Husted , who is facing a bitter election in Ohio against former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown, the bill passed with overwhelming support in the House.
However, many Senate Democrats say the legislation is toothless, and doesn’t do enough to actually hold companies building datacenters responsible for the rise in electricity bills for local communities.
Senator Mark Warner , a Virginia Democrat, called the bill a “fig leaf”, while Chuck Schumer , the Senate minority leader, called it a “fraud” and pointed to the fact it’s entirely optional.
“Instead of trying to score cheap political points with hollow proposals, Senate Republicans need to work with us to take meaningful action that will actually contain these existential risks,” Schumer said this week on the Senate floor.
Following the news that the supreme court has ruled in the Trump administration’s favor, and allowed deportations to so called “third-countries” to continue, Burundi has agreed to join a group of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries who have been deported from the US.
Officials in Bujumbura, Burundi’s economic capital, said they would only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links. There are no details yet on the number of deportees Burundi will take or the financial deal the country has struck with the US.
The Trump administration has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to some half ​a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely. The Guardian has previously reported on the murky deals Washington has struck with various countries to send deportees.
Rachel Leingang and Riley Messer
Some of the biggest food and agriculture corporations in the US are funding a campaign that pays social media influencers to combat elements of Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again platform, according to an investigation by the Guardian and Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project.
The ascension of RFK Jr to secretary of health and human services has boosted his putative campaign to end chronic illness in the US, which he believes is primarily caused by processed foods and dyes, exposure to certain chemicals, and poor farming practices, along with an overuse of what he falsely claims are dangerous vaccines. The “Maha” movement blends long-running mainstream concerns about food and farm safety with conspiracy theories about everything from medicine to milk. A Maha “ summit ” in Washington this week will feature JD Vance and several members of Trump’s cabinet.
A KFF poll from May 2026 reveals that some Maha themes resonate with a broad segment of US adults. About four in 10 say they support the Maha movement, while a majority of the public say there is not enough regulation of pesticides used in agriculture (64%) or of chemical food additives (75%).
Cross-partisan support in Washington on some of these issues poses a threat to the food industry’s bottom line – though the Trump administration has largely stopped short of enacting new regulations.
But several large corporations are fighting back. An effort by the Center for Food Integrity, an industry-funded non-profit, tracks public sentiment around key issues central to Maha and suggests ways that agricultural interests can counter those narratives by appealing to emotion or scientific reasoning.

articles.title_orig: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.
In his first party conference speech as prime minister, he announced plans for a national commission to explore options for electoral reform.
He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".
He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".
Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.
Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.
Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.
In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote or less."
He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."
Burnham did not set out details of who would lead his proposed commission, or when it would begin its work.
Any move to change the voting system would be supported by the Liberal Democrats, who had previously urged Burnham to introduce proportional representation before the next election, which must be held by 2029.
However, any move away from first-past-the-post is likely to be resisted by the Conservatives. Reform UK backed introducing PR at the last election, but there has been speculation that its enthusiasm for the move may have since cooled.
Speaking to broadcasters after Burnham's speech, Reform leader Nigel Farage said he was open to debating a potential change to the system "at some point" but other issues were "far more urgent".
He added: "Is this an absolute priority for the general election after the next one? I don't believe that it is."
Support for changing the voting system is also not universal within Labour, with deputy leader Lucy Powell acknowledging that "parts of the Labour Party" are not in favour of it.
Speaking to Politics Live on BBC 2, she said she personally backed electoral reform but declined to specify a proposed new system, adding there were "lots of models" available.
At the last UK election the Liberal Democrats backed the introduction of a single transferable vote (STV) system, which is used for Scottish council elections.
Other options include the additional member system, a hybrid model that combines first-past-the-post with regional party lists that is used to elect members of the Scottish Parliament.
Earlier this year, the Welsh Senedd was elected for the first time using a closed-list proportional representation system .
The Green Party supports electoral reform but Green MP Ellie Chowns said: "The PM cannot acknowledge the unfairness of a system capable of handing power to a government with a minority of the vote share, and then say the answer is to let that happen exactly once more before he fixes it.
"Burnham must act with urgency to immediately jumpstart the National Commission, guarantee timely progress, and ensure its recommendations are delivered in time for a fairer voting system to be in place at the next general election."

articles.title_orig: What we know about the Cornell University frat house rape investigation
articles.title_zh: What we know about the Cornell University frat house rape investigation
articles.content_orig:
Some violent protesters allegedly torched police cars parked on the highway on Sunday
One of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence.
Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation.
Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack.
But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad.
Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus.
Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised.
By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed.
University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home.
Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate.
Lovely Professional University has suspended classes for 10 days amid violent protests
The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier.
The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed.
BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered.
Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge.
Behind the gates, students described a night of fear.
"We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here."
Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here."
Arya, a student at the college, says they thought about nothing but leaving the campus on the night of violence
That the police open a case and investigate the allegation was among the protesters' central demands.
"The students have been demanding that an FIR  [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC.
Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred.
Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room.
"As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said.
But they are continuing to examine the footage.
"The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this."
Protesting students had earlier blocked a nearby highway which was opened later on Monday
It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself.
There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university.
"We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield."
Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played.
Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own.
On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them.
The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations.
Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the recent suicide of a female LPU student from Telangana state. Police say investigations into her death had already begun and there is no verified evidence linking the two cases.
There is heavy police presence around the university campus since the unrest
For now, life on campus has been interrupted. Regular classes have been suspended for 10 days and exams postponed. Students have been asked to return home after consulting their parents or guardians.
Those who are staying have been advised to stay in their residences and avoid further unrest.
The Punjab State Women's Commission has also sought the FIR, details of the investigation and information about arrangements for students' safety.
The investigation now has two separate questions to answer: whether there is evidence of the assault that set the protests in motion? And who was responsible for the violence that followed?
Addressing the students on Monday, LPU's pro-chancellor Rashmi Mittal said she was hurt that despite the university's many channels for students to raise concerns, they had instead "believed the rumour that was spreading". She also alleged that outsiders had joined the unrest.
"I feel students can't do this," she said.

articles.title_orig: A startup wants to build a massive nuclear-powered data center on public land in Utah
articles.title_zh: A startup wants to build a massive nuclear-powered data center on public land in Utah
articles.content_orig:
A Valar Atomics microreactor is seen on a C-17 aircraft, without nuclear fuel, at March Air Reserve Base in California on Feb. 15. The reactor was transported from March Air Reserve Base to Hill Air Force Base in Utah. Matthew Daly/AP hide caption
A startup whose founder has vowed to "make nuclear great again" is planning to place hundreds of reactors on federal land in Utah, according to documents reviewed exclusively by NPR.
Valar Atomics is planning what it calls "Project Beehive" on over 9,000 acres of land held under the Bureau of Land Management near Price, Utah. The facility would include data centers and some 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and others for storing nuclear waste, according to a proposal from the company to federal regulators.
In aggregate, the reactors would produce around 9.6 gigawatts of power for the data centers and even more thermal heat for other industrial applications. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces only around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average (though its peak capacity in summer can reach around 10 gigawatts).
The project's timeline calls for nonnuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028.
Valar has also sought the use of around 650 acres of state land as part of the same project, according to state records . The Salt Lake Tribune first reported on the project's use of state land last week, but not the much larger proposed use of federal lands.
The project has raised alarm among local activists, who are already facing a slew of data center proposals in the state.
"It's concerning to see that the Trump administration, with the support of the state of Utah, is pushing this forward on significant acreage of public lands," said Neal Clark, wildlands director at the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, a Utah-based nonprofit that seeks to protect public lands.
"The coalition of people who are concerned about these things completely transcends political lines," added Lexi Tuddenham, the executive director of the Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah, which has tracked nuclear-related industries in the state. Tuddenham said that at the moment her primary goal is to raise awareness. "The biggest thing we can do right now is to let people know about it."
In a written statement, the Bureau of Land Management's Utah office confirmed it had received an application from the company.
"We are currently reviewing the application for completeness," it told NPR in an email. As the application moves through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, "we will make sure the public has meaningful opportunities to provide input," it added.
Valar did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment. In an interview with NPR in July, Valar CEO Isaiah Taylor said his company was committed to safety and community engagement. "We're doing it responsibly and accountably to this community," he said of a smaller test reactor that the company was operating in a neighboring county.
Project Beehive reveals the scale of the ambitions held by a new generation of companies planning a comeback for nuclear power. The companies are backed by the Trump administration, which has enacted a slew of regulatory reforms over the past year and a half to make their "small modular reactors" easier to test and build.
Valar Atomics CEO Isaiah Taylor (right) and Energy Secretary Chris Wright (left) stand behind President Trump as he makes an announcement on American nuclear innovation on July 24. Valar has been both an advocate of reforming nuclear regulations and a beneficiary of changes made by the Trump administration. Eric Lee/Getty Images hide caption
Valar has been both closely involved with those reforms and a beneficiary of them. Taylor was in the room when President Trump signed a series of executive orders last year designed to accelerate the development of nuclear power, and his company was accepted into the Department of Energy's Reactor Pilot Program in August 2025. This past February, the U.S. military flew Valar's test reactor from California to Utah aboard a C-17 transport aircraft.
The reactor, known as Ward 250, received rapid approval this year after the Department of Energy conducted a quiet overhaul of its internal safety and security regulations for nuclear reactors. It achieved criticality by reaching a self-sustaining nuclear reaction in June , in a tentlike structure in the Utah desert about 30 miles from the site of Project Beehive.
At a press event on July 1, the company marked another milestone when it used Ward 250 to produce electricity. Taylor powered up the test reactor and used a simple thermoelectric system to run a single Nvidia microchip.
"Ladies and gentlemen, Valar Atomics just became the first startup in history to make nuclear electricity right here," he told the crowd.
The scale of Project Beehive vastly outstrips that July demonstration. Since the turn of the century, the U.S. has switched on just three new nuclear power plants, producing a total of around 3.4 gigawatts of electricity. Those reactors are far larger than the small modular reactors that Valar plans to use, and each costs many billions of dollars to build.
Valar and other companies are hoping to upend the nuclear business model because small reactors can be mass-produced and placed in series, like a set of nuclear batteries. Valar's 25-megawatt electric units could be installed one at a time, allowing Project Beehive to be built in phases over a number of years. That in turn would reduce the cost and allow the site to enter operation relatively quickly. According to a document reviewed by NPR, the full site could be completed by 2032.
Tuddenham said she thinks the use of federal lands for such a project is unprecedented. "In this case, I think it's bigger than the local community," she said. "If we have facilities like this on public land for waste storage, for massive nuclear development, for data centers, that's going to have tremendous implications for how public lands are used."

SAN DIEGO -- They packed Petco Park anticipating a party in the Gaslamp on Tuesday night. The Cubs could do little to stop it. The Padres wouldn't let it end.
Three pitches into the top of the first inning, Michael King punched out Pete Crow-Armstrong. The ballpark erupted. Eight pitches later, King had retired the side in order. Louder, still. Leading off the bottom of the first, Fernando Tatis Jr. crushed the first pitch he saw over the center-field wall. Somehow, even louder.
That noise reached a crescendo two batters later, when Manny Machado launched another home run off Cubs left-hander Matthew Boyd . The Padres were well on their way to an 8-0 victory in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series. The party in downtown San Diego never stopped.
“The crowd was great,” said Cubs manager Craig Counsell. “... They had a lot to cheer about tonight -- and we didn't give them anything to be quiet about.”
King would carry a no-hitter into the seventh. By the time Nico Hoerner broke up King’s bid at history with a soft single down the third-base line with one out in the seventh, the Padres had built a 7-0 lead. It was the longest individual postseason no-hit bid since Aníbal Sánchez went 7 2/3 for the Nationals in the 2019 NLCS. King would finish with seven innings of one-hit ball.
Postseason Guide • Final bracket • Wild Card Series matchups • How to watch Wild Card Series on NBC, Peacock • Postseason schedule
King would allow just that one hit over seven innings -- 28 years to the day that Kevin Brown punched out 16 Astros in the 1998 NLDS. That game is widely regarded as the greatest single-game pitching performance in franchise history. King made a strong case for No. 2.
The game stood in stark contrast to last year’s Wild Card Series between these two teams, which Chicago controlled throughout. Suddenly, the Cubs’ backs are against the wall. And the Padres are one win from a trip to Milwaukee and the NLDS.
“Obviously we've got to continue doing it,” Machado said. “Not all games are going to be like the one today. But we're always ready for the battle.”
Here are some takeaways from Game 1:
1. This is a very different Padres offense
Maybe a few of the names are the same. But this is not the Padres offense that scored all of five runs across three games in last year’s Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field.
For a month now, the Padres have been the best offense in baseball. And if there were any doubt whether that would carry over into October … the Padres erased it with a couple swings in the bottom of the first inning.
"We’re one. We’re coming together as one group," Tatis said. "At-bat after at-bat, we trust each other."
Tatis and Machado became the first Padres teammates to combine for multiple home runs in the first inning of a playoff game in franchise history. Xander Bogaerts would add a homer of his own in the fourth. The Padres poured it on.
By the fifth inning Tuesday night they’d scored more than they had in that entire three-game series at Wrigley Field a year ago.
“We did a good job with Tatis last year,” Counsell said. “We did not do a good job today, and it starts with that.”
Indeed, Tatis struggled last postseason -- and seemed to be at the center of everything on Tuesday night. But beyond that, the Padres offense is just … deeper this year. There are more levers to pull, and Stammen has been pulling them.
2. Boyd’s changeup betrays him
One of the keys to Boyd being as effective and consistent as he has been for the Cubs is the reliability of his changeup. It is his signature offspeed offering, but the lefty’s command of the pitch eluded him in Game 1 and it proved costly.
All three home runs surrendered by Boyd came off his changeup, marking the first time in his career (regular season or postseason) that he allowed that many homers in a game off that pitch. The blasts from Tatis, Machado and Bogaerts each came off changeups that were left in the strike zone.
“When it comes down to it, I just wasn’t as sharp with my changeup,” Boyd said. “It could have been better. They definitely could’ve been better. A team like that, especially Machado and Tatis, they’re going to be aggressive. I just didn’t throw it where I wanted to and they hit the mistakes.”
While allowing homers was an issue for the Cubs’ staff this season – their 231 homers surrendered led the NL – Boyd was one of the better performers on that front. In fact, the lefty allowed no homers in September, only two in his final seven starts combined and only allowed two or more in a game in three of his 22 starts.
3. Michael King might’ve done more than just win Game 1
The Padres have the sport's best bullpen. But how much stress could it handle across three games this week?
Well, now they really only need to worry about two -- at most.
Not only was King electric. The fact that he covered seven innings -- not to mention the tack-on runs from the Padres offense -- could go a long way toward helping them win the series. Mason Miller and Adrian Morejon are still fresh. The whole bullpen is, really.
The Cubs’ uphill climb in Games 2 and 3 just got a whole lot steeper. A red-hot Nick Pivetta gets the ball in Game 2 -- and Stammen can turn to his high-leverage arms whenever he needs to.
4. Cubs needed their lineup to step up
The Cubs ended the season leading the Major Leagues in runs scored (850), walks (674), slugging percentage (.428) and OPS (.767), while pacing the NL in home runs (220). A deep October run was going to be contingent on that offense continuing to roll, given the rocky nature of Chicago’s pitching.
Game 1 against the Padres could not have gone worse in that regard for the North Siders. The Cubs went 0-for-20 into the seventh inning before Hoerner’s infield single. Chicago’s dynamic one-two punch of Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman finished a combined 0-for-7 with six strikeouts.
“He was really good. Tip your cap,” Bregman said of King. “He threw the ball really well. Had everything really working and we didn’t do, really, anything right today. The good news is we get to show up tomorrow and play a baseball game. We’ve just got to execute better in all phases of the game.”

Backpack, the winning bear, after months of eating to gain weight ahead of hibernating in winter.
A brown bear known as 89 Backpack has won the annual Fat Bear Week competition, after what the US National Parks Service described as a "battle of size, skill, snack acquisition, and strategic loafing".
Backpack's wideness narrowly defeated a bear known only as 910, earning 103,344 votes to 910's 98,253 in the final round of the competition, which is run by the Katmai National Park in Alaska.
The National Parks Service thanked the 16 bears who "involuntarily participated" in the competition, now in its thirteenth year.
Backpack, who was described by one supporter as having both the "chonk and the badonk", will shortly enter hibernation, which can last up to six months.
His mother Holly was the 2019 Fat Bear Week winner. Backpack's name derives not from what another supporter described as the "light bulb shape" of his body, but his habit, as a cub, of climbing onto Holly's back when she waded through the park's salmon-filled Brooks River.
Another supporter described him as being a "big fuzzy boy".
But Backpack was not without his detractors. One person said she felt that Bear 910, a female who raised both her biological cub and an adopted niece, was a "larger bear all around. Backpack just has a bigger booty".
"I just feel like 910 really put in the work this year," another 910 fan wrote on the park's Facebook page, while a voter commented, "She round, she thick my girl 910 got my vote."
Fat Bear Week: Which bear has put on the most weight?
The finalists' latest weights have not yet been revealed. But adult male brown bears average up to 408kg in mid-summer and often pack on the equivalent of 25% of their body weight by autumn. The largest males can weigh more than 540kg .
Females are smaller but can reach weights of over 300kg. Cubs are born weighing roughly half a kilogram.
"During hibernation, bears do not eat or drink and lose one-third of their body weight. Their winter survival depends on accumulating ample fat reserves before entering the den," organisers wrote.
From June until mid October, the bears gorge on food, including salmon caught with their jaws or paws.
Backpack's biography says his "quiet toughness has allowed him to find his niche alongside the biggest bears at Brooks River".
Last year, over 1.7 million votes were cast from more than 100 countries to crown the competition's heavyweight champion.

articles.title_zh: Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to 'self-police' AI development
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump speaks to reporters at the White House in Washington, Tuesday Sept. 29, 2026, after meeting with top executives of AI firms, as House Speaker Mike Johnson of La., and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang listen. Jacquelyn Martin/AP hide caption
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Tuesday said that he and a large group of leaders of artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews during a meeting at the White House aimed at addressing Americans' fears about the technology.
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.
Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson met with leading executives from top tech firms that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centers in communities across the country, which have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition.
The accord was signed by Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk, founder of xAI, which is now part of SpaceX.
The accord, which Trump posted on his social media site, Truth Social, late Tuesday, opened the door to future regulation but focused on four voluntary steps for the companies to take.
The accord said the companies would implement "robust internal controls," partner with an "independent external auditor" to assess whether the controls were working, and establish a committee within each company's board of directors to evaluate reports from internal and external auditors.
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations," the accord said.
Trump repeatedly praised the business executives for developing a technology that he said would produce "unbelievable growth." Investment in data centers and the accompanying computer equipment has accelerated the economy and boosted the stock market, which has swelled investment accounts for higher-income Americans and lifted their spending.
Yet there were some notes of caution Tuesday. Amodei, who has been one of the most outspoken voicescalling for a slowdown in AI development, said, "The technology has very real risks."
"And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei said.
Trump suggested that about 10 people would be named to a committee to "watch over the whole enterprise" and said the accord would be "morally binding." He also said he would name someone to oversee the agreement in coming days after consulting with industry.
Some of the actions outlined in the accord are measures these companies are already taking in some form or have previously committed to doing.
The intention of the accord balances the latitude needed for innovation with regulation, said Shri Narayanan, a university professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Southern California. That innovation is not just limited to improving the capabilities of these AI models, Narayanan said, but also to efforts to improve model safety and security.
Other experts are skeptical of putting "so much faith in self-policing," like Robin Jia, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Southern California. Jia said it's crucial to ensure the leading labs' intentions are "well-aligned with the broader interest of the American public." He pointed to the recent disclosures of hacking incidents and said: "As the models get better, the consequences of such things are only going to get greater."
Some also took issue with the accord's vague, broad language. Alex Pascal, executive director of the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society, said: "The only way to reduce the risks and harms of AI to Americans is through robust legal liability, regulation and fundamentally changing the race dynamics that are driving unsafe decision-making by frontier AI developers whose costs are borne by the American people."
Huang sat to Trump's right during a White House luncheon meeting, according to a seating chart the president posted on Truth Social. Musk sat to Trump's left.
Earlier Tuesday, Trump promised that the U.S. government wouldn't limit the development of artificial intelligence or support calls for "guardrails" or other restrictions.
"I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," Trump said at the unveiling of an AI chatbot, America.gov, intended to help Americans navigate government services. "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot."
The unveiling of the AI government chatbot occurred at a daylong event in Washington during which multiple Trump administration officials celebrated a "Golden Age" fueled by what Trump insists on calling "super intelligence," rather than artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio highlighted that the chatbot at America.gov could soon be used to apply for a first-time passport fully online, without the in-person visit to a processing center currently required.
Trump also said the executives had agreed to assuage the bipartisan opposition to data centers cropping up in local communities across the country by providing more financial support to local schools or taking steps to reduce energy costs.
"You're going to see, data centers are going to be very popular," Trump said. If the opposition continued, Trump suggested, "they'll be forced to go overseas or other locations."
Also Tuesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a television interview that the company is increasingly focused on safety. The day before, his company halted the rollout of a new model over safety concerns.
"We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model," he said on CNBC. "We have to do these in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don't have a bunch of anxiety."
For his part, Trump on Tuesday portrayed the race to develop AI as largely a global competition between the United States and China. He said there would be a winner and a loser, with no "second place."
The two countries agreed last week to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington. But Trump underscored Tuesday that he didn't want to cooperate too much with China: "I didn't want to do anything, because we're leading. Why would I want to do anything?"

By JAMES TAPSFIELD, UK POLITICAL EDITOR
Published: 02:38 EDT, 30 September 2026 | Updated: 05:40 EDT, 30 September 2026
Andy Burnham is facing a Labour backlash as he hints at going 'all the way' and pledging to rejoin the EU.
The PM used his big conference speech yesterday to blame Brexit for many of the country's problems, saying he will spell out options for the future at a summit with Brussels later this year.
But the move has sparked concerns among his own troops, with Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra warning returning to the bloc is 'unrealistic'.
The stance also represents a dramatic U-turn from May, when Mr Burnham told a conference in Leeds: 'I am not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU.
'I respect the decision that was made at the referendum and it is going to undermine everything I have said about strengthening democracy if we don't respect that vote.'
In interviews after his speech yesterday, Mr Burnham told the BBC he did not want to leave the issue 'hanging' and he wanted to be clear on 'where we want Britain to go in the next decade'.
Asked whether he wanted the UK to rejoin the bloc, he told Radio 4's Today programme he wanted to 'look at the options'.
Andy Burnham is facing a Labour backlash as he hints at going 'all the way' and pledging to rejoin the EU
'We could stay as we are. That's definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay,' he told the programme.
'We could look at what (former Conservative chancellor) George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market or we could go all the way.'
Labour's election manifesto in 2024 ruled out joining a customs union, going back into the single market or allowing the return of freedom of movement with the EU.
But Mr Burnham has indicated he is prepared to recommend going beyond those red lines in future.
'There are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each,' he told the BBC.
He said the need for a debate about the UK's future relationship with Europe was part of his plan to shift the country in a new direction.
'We've been in a rut. The country hasn't been working for people as it should,' he told BBC Breakfast.
Tory Deputy Leader Alex Burghart said: 'You cannot trust a word Andy Burnham says.
'Just a few weeks ago he said he wanted to move on from the Brexit arguments and now he is dragging Britain back into them by floating the prospect of rejoining the EU.
'Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions. While they look backwards, the Conservatives will look forwards.'

articles.content_orig:
PM says he is looking at all options and ministers will examine ‘what is doable’ and the ‘pros and cons’
UK politics live – latest updates
Andy Burnham has opened the door to the UK rejoining the EU, saying Britain could “go all the way”, as he prepares to reconsider Labour’s post-Brexit red lines.
The prime minister used a series of interviews after his emotional Labour conference speech to spell out how wide-ranging his consideration of Britain’s future with Brussels could be because Brexit had caused “more harm than good”.
Burnham said the government could keep the current arrangements, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” in what would be full EU membership. Speaking to the BBC, he said ministers would examine “what is doable” and the “pros and cons” of each option.
Asked whether he wanted the UK to rejoin the bloc, the prime minister told Radio 4’s Today programme he wanted to “look at the options”. He added: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market or we could go all the way.”
It is a significant shift from the position Labour fought the 2024 election on. Its manifesto explicitly ruled out returning to the EU single market or customs union, as well as restoring freedom of movement.
A customs union would bring Britain much closer to the EU on trade in goods. The UK and EU would apply the same tariffs to imports from elsewhere, removing trade barriers businesses have faced after Brexit . But it would not on its own put Britain back inside the wider single market or remove every border check.
If Britain were to rejoin the single market, it would be a significant step with the country having to accept closer alignment with EU rules.
“There are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each,” Burnham told the BBC.
Although Burnham has not set out any timetables or specifics, to “go all the way” would mean considering EU membership. He went further in his interviews on Wednesday than his conference speech in which he told delegates Britain could not keep avoiding a decision about its long-term relationship with its largest trading partner.
The prime minister has vowed to set out different choices facing the country around the time of the UK-EU summit in November. “We’ve been in a rut. The country hasn’t been working for people as it should,” he told BBC Breakfast. The summit was originally supposed to take place in July under Keir Starmer but was postponed after his resignation.
after newsletter promotion
While Britain will take part in the Erasmus + scheme again in 2027, the EU has authorised talks at the summit on closer electricity-market links, with negotiations on food trade and youth mobility still under way.
Burnham argued in his conference speech that leaving the EU had weakened Britain’s cooperation with EU countries on migration and said the summit would assess how the two parties could work more closely. “We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of the century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market,” Burnham said in his speech on Tuesday in Liverpool.
“I cannot say to you that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners. And there are different options.”
The prime minister was more cautious when pressed on help households could receive in the budget given the looming winter and rising energy and fuel costs. Burnham said he was considering “everything that might help people” including whether to scrap panned fuel duty increases.
“The question I’ve got is: ‘How many can I afford?’” he told BBC Breakfast. The chancellor, John Healey, has said “fiscal discipline” will be at the heart of his budget despite facing calls to offer people more help with the cost of living.

articles.title_orig: Trump, top AI leaders agree to voluntary ​AI ​standards
articles.title_zh: Trump, top AI leaders agree to voluntary ​AI ​standards
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., discusses President Donald Trump’s meeting with artificial intelligence leaders at the White House and the signing of the White House Accord on SI on ‘The Bottom Line.’
President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed an executive order directing the federal government to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "Super Intelligence" across the executive branch, cementing a rebranding effort he has championed in recent weeks.
Signed after a White House summit with leading technology executives, the order directs federal agencies to use the terms "Super Intelligence" and "SI" in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents and other non-statutory materials.
The order also directs agencies to "no longer acknowledge" the terms " artificial intelligence " and "AI," according to the White House.
The order further instructs the assistant to the president for science and technology to develop a federal definition of SI and recommend any additional executive actions needed to implement the new terminology.
TRUMP TO MAKE SURPRISE STOP AT TEXAS TRUCK FACTORY TO TOUT MANUFACTURING
President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed an executive order directing the federal government to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "Super Intelligence" across the executive branch. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Trump argued in the order that AI no longer reflects the technology's rapidly advancing capabilities, saying SI better captures its promise and potential.
"The term 'Super Intelligence' more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies," Trump wrote.
He also wrote that modern AI systems are increasingly amplifying human ingenuity and unlocking new forms of creativity, arguing they represent the beginning of a new era of SI.
The order follows remarks Trump made at last week's United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where he publicly called for replacing the term "artificial intelligence" with SI.
TRUMP SAYS HE APPROVED NEW FUEL ECONOMY STANDARDS ENDING BIDEN-ERA ELECTRIC VEHICLE MANDATE
Trump signed the executive order after a White House summit with leading technology executives. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this, and now I say whoever wins SI, whoever wins superintelligence, wins. That's the group that wins," Trump said at the time.
The executive order also comes as governments and technology companies continue debating how rapidly advancing AI systems should be governed.
During a White House roundtable with tech executives, Trump, who has opposed imposing formal guardrails on SI, said participants signed a document at the conclusion of the gathering.
Trump added that the document, dubbed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, is "morally binding" for the executives who signed it.
"They almost viewed it as a separate kind of constitution," Trump said of the tech leaders. "When they signed that, it meant a lot."
TRUMP REBRANDS AI, REJECTS 'GLOBALIST SCHEME' TO CONTROL TECH
After the summit, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X Tuesday that he viewed the summit as a "positive step." (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
After Tuesday's White House summit, House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said participants focused on striking "the right balance" between "the interests of the American people," advancing technology and maintaining the United States' competitive edge over China .
"This is a statement of principles that you'll see, a statement of standards, commitments that are voluntary on behalf of the industry. It sets forth expectations," Johnson said. "It's, in short, summary, robust internal controls and layers of internal and external review."
Tuesday evening, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X that he viewed the summit as a "positive step."
"I think it's a significant positive step that the leaders of every major American lab have committed to implementing robust internal controls and multiple layers of audits and reviews," Zuckerberg wrote.

articles.title_orig: China’s R&D spending tops OECD average for first time. What comes next?
articles.title_zh: China’s R&D spending tops OECD average for first time. What comes next?
articles.content_orig:
Beijing plans to double down on basic research, cutting-edge technologies and scientific talent as it strives to achieve tech self-sufficiency
For the first time, China’s spending on research and development as a share of gross domestic product has surpassed the average for Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) members – a trend one analyst expects to continue as Beijing seeks to strengthen technological self-reliance amid intensifying global competition.
R&D expenditure exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan (US$584.8 billion) in 2025, accounting for 2.8 per cent of GDP, Science and Technology Minister Yin Hejun said at a press conference on Tuesday. The OECD average stood at 2.7 per cent for the year, the National Bureau of Statistics reported.
Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said the achievement showed how China’s investment in innovation had reached a level comparable to that of developed economies. He expected the share of GDP devoted to R&D to keep rising, with a greater focus on optimising funding allocation and improving research efficiency.
“We must continuously increase the proportion of investment in basic research to build a solid foundation for ‘zero-to-one’ original breakthroughs,” Wang said, while ensuring that “large-scale R&D investments translate more efficiently into industrial competitiveness”.

articles.title_orig: Man City’s ‘sham contracts’, spending breaches and ‘disguised funding’: Breaking down the findings
articles.title_zh: Man City’s ‘sham contracts’, spending breaches and ‘disguised funding’: Breaking down the findings
articles.content_orig:
Published: 14:33 EDT, 29 September 2026 | Updated: 15:47 EDT, 29 September 2026
It is an episode which illustrates the struggle there has been in extracting transparency and truth about Manchester City , whose relentless, bullying corporate machine has looked to shut down investigation and inquiry through years of deceit.
Eight years ago, I wrote a story, published by The Independent, whom I worked for at the time, about an obscure and puzzling company called Fordham Sports Image Rights, to which City had supposedly sold the club’s future image rights for £24.5million – a sum they needed to avoid breaching financial sustainability rules in the 2012-13 season.
City had made no secret of earning this figure. They stated it in their annual accounts. Yet Fordham’s directors, detailed in their Companies House listing, were City’s very own legal officer Simon Cliff and non-executive director John MacBeath – a qualified chartered accountant.
Fordham clearly had a very distinct link to the club. And when I made more inquiries about City selling off those image rights to such a firm, there were blank looks. Several sources confirmed to me that, contrary to this notion, City were still raking in millions from those deals.
The sources were significant people. A Spanish financier Esteve Calzada, chief executive of Saudi club Al Hilal these days, who as an adviser to City at that time had negotiated image rights deals for Kevin De Bruyne and others, said he was working for the club itself.
Calzada, a good friend of City chief executive Ferran Soriano, told me: ‘I’ve always been working on a commercial arrangement with the club. We help the club bring in deals.’
My sources on the Fordham story included an adviser to City chief executive Ferran Soriano (right, pictured with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak)
Those controlling City’s information are not the only ones you go up against when challenging the notion of Sheikh Mansour (centre) as a beneficent altruist
The detail might seem arcane and dry. The small financial details get crushed these days in the stampede for the next soundbite or headline. But it was fundamental to City's attempts to comply with the rules set out for any teams wishing to compete in the Champions League, at a time when UEFA were investigating the club.
We published the article. ‘Manchester City earning millions from image rights after telling UEFA investigators they had sold them,’ our headline stated.
The full force of Manchester City’s lawyers came down on us in a way which I have not experienced in more than 30 years in this business. There was an immediate threat to sue. A demand from the specialist internet law firm City employed that the digital piece be removed. That an apology for it be published. And that I personally tweet out that apology. It would have been an unprecedented level of 'contrition'.
Ours was not a big operation. As I recall, the managing editor who fielded this, Will Gore, was juggling 1001 tasks and did not have a sea of lawyers in the next office. But we were not cowed. A detailed, 1,500-word defence of the story was sent in return. We waited. And we waited. And we heard no more from Manchester City or their specialist internet lawyers.
In November 2018, a cache of documents extracted by hacker Rui Pinto, and subsequently published, suggested that we actually only had half of the story.
City's owners, Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) were in fact financing Fordham, according to the leaks – effectively paying part of the players' wages through the shell company which had paid City the £24.5m for the ‘image rights’. Not only were City boosting their income against the rules but reducing their headline wage bill as they did so.
Of course, those controlling City’s information are not the only ones you go up against when challenging the fluffy PR notion of Sheikh Mansour as a beneficent altruist. Many's the time that their weaponised supporters have dispensed filth on social media. They still will.
Last Friday’s revelation that City had been found guilty on all but one relatively inconsequential charge was justification for all who have seen through City’s deceit and questioned the absurd notion that they are the victims of some Manchester United and Liverpool led ‘red cartel’.
And, let it be said, justification for the staff of the Premier League, for whom this experience has not been easy. The Premier League, more than any, have refused to be intimidated.
Staff at the Premier League, including CEO Richard Masters, have remained steadfast in their pursuing of the City case despite outside pressure
But when the League’s explosive and utterly damning statement was published late on Tuesday afternoon, there, in the relatively brief summary of how the club had artificially reduced its costs by £900million over nine seasons, was the name: ‘Fordham.’
It was detailed as one of the ‘sham arrangements’, entered into to enable City to ‘record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred.’ Yes, the statement related, there had been ‘a “sham” circular arrangement with Fordham.'
This was a rather more succinct and emphatic way of putting it than we accomplished in November 2018 for an article that was never removed and is still very much there . We were right all along and despite the mess, waste and ugliness of this interminable case, there is a sweet kind of vindication about that.
