articles.title_zh: Why Caitlin Clark was at the center of a Hawks-Hawkeyes mix-up during Senate argument - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Special counsel Jack Smith, who brought two indictments against now-President Donald Trump in 2023, testified in front of Congress again on Tuesday — this time, to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Smith’s testimony comes as Republicans continue to probe the investigations into Trump and as some in the party, including the president, have pushed for often-unspecified criminal charges to be brought against Smith.
Here are the major takeaways from Tuesday’s hearing.
Republicans have struggled mightily to substantiate Trump’s desire for Smith to be charged criminally . But rarely has it seemed to backfire like it did Tuesday .
Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri crafted an apparent conspiracy theory about Smith being tied to the prosecution of Trump in Fulton County, Georgia. To substantiate his theory, Schmitt cited text messages he suggested showed Smith had been at an Atlanta Hawks game on February 3, 2024 – the day after Fulton County prosecutor Fani Willis and special prosecutor Nathan Wade admitted to an affair.
Smith appeared dumbfounded, though. He denied going to a Hawks game and said he had no recollection of even being in Atlanta.
“What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta at a Warriors-Hawks game on February 3, 2024 – the day after Willis and Wade announced their affair?” Schmitt said.
Schmitt went big on the allegation, telling Smith, “I don’t think you know that we have this stuff.” He urged Smith not to “perjure yourself.” He later called Smith a “dirtbag.” He later told the “Charlie Kirk Show” that he was just asking questions and seeing whether Smith would ensnare himself.
Eventually, Democrats got Schmitt to allow Smith to actually review the evidence – a poster featuring the texts in question. In one of them, a fellow prosecutor asks about a seat being reserved for Smith. The poster showed the Atlanta Hawks’ arena.
But by this point, Smith seemed to put it together. He said he was not at a game featuring the Atlanta Hawks , but rather the University of Iowa Hawkeyes women’s basketball team – which then featured Caitlin Clark – at the University of Maryland in the Washington, DC, area.
Smith’s recollection matches up with a game played that day.
Behind the scenes, a source familiar with how Schmitt got it wrong told CNN the Republican senator checked what men’s college and NBA games were scheduled that day and found only the Atlanta Hawks set to play — but he failed to consider that Smith may have been at a women’s basketball game.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, after clearing up the matter, said Schmitt should apologize.
Instead, he laughed it off, telling CNN later Tuesday: “Who knew Jack Smith was a Caitlin Clark fan?”
The Republican defended his pointed line of questioning, saying, “That’s what these hearings are for. You ask questions, you get answers. You know, Jack Smith has perjured himself before, but if he says he’s at the game, maybe he’s a Caitlin Clark fan. We’ll accept that.”
At the hearing, he maintained that the texts “could have obviously been related to the prosecution” in Fulton County. He said he stood by calling Smith a “dirtbag.”
The scene epitomized how speculative and thinly constructed the GOP’s allegations about Smith, Trump’s foes and about the justice system being weaponized against Trump have been. Likewise, the GOP’s other major perjury allegation against Smith rests on a complete misreading of the evidence .
But rarely has this apparent fishing expedition been laid so bare. Schmitt seemed to firmly believe he had nailed Smith on something. But just minutes later, it seemed to fall apart – and rather spectacularly so.
Smith is a very careful witness. He often pauses noticeably before answering a question — in a way that can be a little jarring.
But he’s also made clear that he wants to fight back against the Trump administration’s weaponization of the justice system against people like him. And on Tuesday, he was a little more animated and open.
He punctuated his opening statement by saying, “Fear may be contagious; courage is as well.”
He also called it an “outrage” that people he worked with were “targeted illegally, lost their jobs illegally, and had their lives turned upside down by this Department of Justice.”
When asked about the Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling conferring presidents with a large degree of immunity, Smith said it “can be very dangerous for the rule of law” for powerful people to benefit from such exceptions.
He also jousted with lawmakers a little more than he did before, rather than dryly reciting facts.
When GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas asked him whether he had any regrets, Smith said he regretted that “the people I worked with have been unfairly fired and vilified.”
When  Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina claimed Smith unfairly targeted the phone records of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, Smith told her that Lindsey Graham had investigated Trump’s underlying voter-fraud claims and found them to be false.
And he said he won’t be going away quietly.
“I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the president or others,” Smith said.
That exchange with Darline Graham was also significant when it comes to learning something new about the attempted prosecutions of Trump.
The reason: Smith said Lindsey Graham was likely to be a witness in the case.
“I believe your brother was a patriotic public servant,” Smith said. “He was not a target of our investigation. In fact, he likely would have been a witness in our case. Your brother investigated the claims that Donald Trump was making. He found them to be false.”
Lindsey Graham publicly broke with Trump on the Senate floor after January 6 (i.e. “ count me out ”) and appeared to be initially helpful to investigators probing the situation.
He later reconciled with Trump and assailed Smith’s investigation when he was among those whose phone records were wrapped up in the probe — and even pushed to get a financial payout for it.
Smith’s comments suggest Graham could have played at least some role in proving the charges against Trump.
The former special counsel seemed to make a point to repeatedly vouch for members of his former staff  who were fired by Trump’s Justice Department and, in some cases, were repeatedly invoked by name at Tuesday’s hearing.
Smith even called them “heroes.”
“My view: These people are heroes, and I believe our country does not recognize and pay enough attention to people like that,” he said. “I think if we did, the partisan things that we’re discussing today – a lot of that would go away.”
Smith also warned about what ousting people like that would portend for the country.
“If you drive those people out of public service, the institutions we rely on for justice, for protecting our country — those institutions are weakened,” Smith said.
When Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff of California talked about how Smith had been attacked, Smith said it was “much more important that the public servants who I work with – that we stop vilifying public servants.”
It’s been nearly a year since Trump appeared alongside then-Attorney General Pam Bondi and claimed Smith had committed crimes.
“Hopefully the Attorney General is looking at what he’s done,” Trump added eight months ago on social media.
There’s been little since then to suggest the Trump administration is able to provide him what he wants. And Tuesday’s hearing often felt like going through the motions more so than anything else.
Apart from Schmitt’s attempt at a gotcha, other Republican lawmakers generally mined territory already covered in the January House Judiciary Committee hearing .
Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri and others repeated an allegation from months ago that Smith perjured himself with his denials about seeking the contents of lawmakers’ communications. But Smith pointed to the holes in that previously debunked theory.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up
articles.content_orig:
Millions of taxpayer dollars have already been spent on President Donald Trump’s hagiographic ads, according to estimates by a leading political ad-tracking firm. And a total of $20 million has been allocated for the effort, which watchdog groups have deemed illegal.
The TV airtime for the three different Trump ads has cost at least $2.5 million to date, the ad-tracking firm AdImpact told CNN.
The actual cost of the taxpayer-funded ad campaign is even higher, but can’t be fully ascertained.
The money for these ads is coming from Customs and Border Protection, or CBP for short, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN.
Earlier this month, the White House Office of Management and Budget, led by Russell Vought, allocated $20 million to CBP for what it called “OBBBA commemorative events.” (OBBBA is an abbreviation for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in 2025.)
Shortly after the $20 million was allocated, CBP contracted an advertising company, LMD Agency Inc., for a national media campaign in the same dollar amount. Days later, the ads began to appear on national television, two additional sources told CNN. LMD’s parent company, MarCom Group, did not respond to CNN’s request for comment.
CBP is an agency within the Department of Homeland Security. On Tuesday, two Democratic senators, Patty Murray and Chris Murphy, sent a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin accusing the department of “a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars.”
The propagandistic ads also faced a fresh challenge from the government watchdog group Public Citizen on Tuesday.
The ads “appear to violate the federal law against using taxpayer funds to finance propaganda and related provisions of the appropriations laws as well as the Hatch Act,” Public Citizen co-presidents Robert Weissman and Lisa Gilbert and the group’s lobbyist, Craig Holman, wrote in a complaint to the Federal Communications Commission and the Federal Trade Commission.
It’s unclear whether any outside groups have the legal standing to sue the Trump administration over the ads.
And while lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have questioned their legality, Republicans — who currently control both the House and the Senate — have not acted.
AdImpact’s analysis for CNN found 2,766 total ad airings between September 23 and 29. The ads have aired on Fox News and the big four broadcast networks.
About 30% of the ad spend has been dedicated to NFL and college football games, according to the firm’s research.
The ads have also appeared during shows like ABC’s “The View,” CBS’s “Elsbeth” and NBC’s “The Weakest Link.”
Because the spots have been classified as a “public service announcement” rather than a traditional political ad buy, the exact spending is not publicly disclosed or verifiable. AdImpact’s estimates are based on air dates, times, local markets, and other factors.
The firm said the first Trump ad to air, featuring the song “Love Me” by JMSN, has aired on more than 1,300 occasions so far.
Lawyers for JMSN sent a cease-and-desist letter to the White House earlier this week, demanding that the administration no longer use the song.
The text “Paid for by the US Government” is seen on screen at the end of each of the three ads, including one repurposed version of an ad from Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.
The “paid for” disclosure conflicts with the administration’s insistence that the ads are “public service announcements” akin to those that past administrations have aired about Medicare, Obamacare and Covid-19 vaccinations.
For actual public service announcements, the TV airtime is usually donated.
Public Citizen argued in its FCC and FTC complaint that the Trump ads “do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program.”
The ads were created in-house by the White House video team, two Trump advisers told CNN, and were personally driven by the president, who was involved in the selection of imagery and videos used, according to a separate source.
The Wall Street Journal first reported where the money came from.
On Tuesday, Public Citizen warned that TV stations could theoretically lose their broadcast licenses for knowingly airing the ads.
“A station knowingly broadcasting illegal, taxpayer-funded partisan propaganda has failed its public interest mandate, forming the basis of a formal license renewal challenge,” they wrote.
The track record of Trump’s FCC, however, shows the agency won’t try to penalize a station for running pro-Trump content. Instead, the agency has challenged ABC’s licenses, a move that many observers have linked to the network’s support for programs like “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” that are harshly critical of the president.
Public Citizen also filed a separate complaint Monday with the Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan agency typically tasked with investigating this type of issue, as well as the US Office of the Special Counsel, calling for an investigation “into who produced these ads and at what cost to taxpayers.”
What constitutes illegal government propaganda, and who can be held accountable for it, is less straightforward.
Propaganda hasn’t been defined in US law, but the Government Accountability Office has identified three categories, including “self-aggrandizement” or “puffery.”
“The most immediate check on this kind of behavior is supposed to be and needs to be Congress. Congress has not asserted itself as the first branch of government with the power of the purse to hold the president accountable,” said Donald Sherman, president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics, or CREW.
GOP lawmakers may be hesitant to provide accountability, he added, because the ads “are designed to boost Republicans in Congress.”
And Hatch Act violations — government officials engaging in partisan political activity while on duty — have largely been dismissed in recent years. Trump administration officials in his first term were alleged to have repeatedly violated the Hatch Act with no penalty. The same was alleged during the Biden administration.
Public Citizen said in a previous statement that it has filed dozens of complaints with the administration about Hatch Act violations, but thinks they have been ignored.

articles.title_orig: 2 Indians Charged In US For Selling Fake Ozempic. They Smuggled It From China
articles.title_zh: 2 Indians Charged In US For Selling Fake Ozempic. They Smuggled It From China
articles.content_orig:
Two Indian nationals have been charged in federal court in Florida with an alleged conspiracy to smuggle counterfeit Ozempic from China in a scheme that purportedly continued even after the Food and Drug Administration seized some of the fake weight-loss drugs in 2023 and warned the public about it, the Department of Justice said Tuesday.
One of the men, 33-year-old Swapnadip Roy, was extradited from Italy and made his initial appearance in U.S. District Court in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday.
Roy and his alleged co-conspirator, Vicky Ramancha, 37, are charged in an indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit smuggling and to defraud the U.S., three counts of smuggling, and two counts of selling counterfeit drugs and holding counterfeit drugs for sale. If convicted, they both face a maximum sentence of 71 years in prison.
Ramancha remains at large.
Court documents state Roy and Ramancha, starting in July 2023 and continuing to the following April, allegedly obtained counterfeit Ozempic from unauthorized sources in China. The popular drug is made by Novo , which recently rebranded from its name Novo Nordisk.
The material they and their co-conspirators allegedly distributed "included counterfeit packaging, package inserts, pen labels, and needles meant to deceive downstream customers into believing they were purchasing authentic Ozempic authorized by the manufacturer," DOJ said.
The newly unsealed indictment says that in July 2023, Ramancha executed a sales and purchase agreement with an unidentified company in Lakeland, Florida, agreeing to supply that company with a product described as being Ozempic "at deeply discounted pricing."
A month later, Ramancha executed another agreement with a company in Sanford, Florida, to supply it with a product described as "Ozempic syringes" at deeply discounted pricing, the indictment alleges.
in November 2023, "Roy utilized threats to facilitate the distribution of product in the United States," writing, "Listen i am not your friend okay? I am not that guy," the indictment alleges.
Roy continued, "I am the guy that will cut some one [expletive] head off and [expletive] peoples dead wives corpse with it," the indictment alleges. "You [expletive] up Solve the [expletive] problem. Get the truck over there today."
After Roy and Ramancha learned that the FDA had seized some of their product that they had distributed in the U.S., a co-conspirator asked Ramancha whether the related FDA warning would affect a pending order to 60,000 additional units of Ozempic, the indictment says.
"Ramancha replied, 'Not at all. But you have to make sure your client are not being idiotic,'" the indictment alleges.
The case comes as the use of so-called GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic for weight loss has become increasingly popular in the U.S.
In July, Gallup reported that the percentage of U.S. adults who take GLP-1 medications for weight loss purposes rose to 11% in  2026, compared to 3% in 2024.
"And 15% report having used the medicine for weight loss at some point, an increase of nine percentage points" over 2024, Gallup noted.
"Counterfeit prescription drugs — especially common ones — threaten the health and safety of every American who depends on the integrity of our pharmaceutical supply," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the DOJ's Criminal Division said in a statement Tuesday.
"These defendants allegedly exploited people's health to pay themselves. We will keep pursuing anyone who seeks to deceive American consumers with counterfeit drugs," Duva said.

articles.title_orig: Trump announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI deal among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’
articles.title_zh: Trump announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI deal among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’
articles.content_orig:
President Trump and the leaders of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies have signed a set of voluntary safety standards, as calls mount for tighter guardrails on AI technology.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Mr. Trump said while flanked by SpaceX's Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Google's Sundar Pichai and a throng of other tech executives.
Following a lunch meeting at the White House , Johnson said the group signed an accord on "super intelligence" — Mr. Trump's preferred term for AI. He described it as a "joint commitment" and "statement of principles" that will voluntarily hold the companies to "robust internal controls."
Asked if the deal was binding, Mr. Trump said: "I think it's morally binding."
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police," the president later said.
The tech companies committed to "four layers of controls and audits" to ensure the AI models are acting as intended, including internal evaluations, audits by an external firm and reviews by each company's board of directors, according to a copy of the one-page accord that Mr. Trump posted to Truth Social . They also agreed to "meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems."
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations," said the accord. "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this."
Mr. Trump said the AI leaders also discussed forming a 10-person committee to "watch over the enterprise." And the president said he plans to name an "AI czar" in the next three or four days.
Also on Tuesday, the president signed an executive order directing the federal government to use the term "Super Intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence.
The rare meeting between competing tech titans followed months of growing concern from researchers, politicians and industry figures that ever-more-powerful AI technology could pose safety risks.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported instances of their AI models going rogue and gaining unauthorized access to other companies' systems, or being used for dangerous purposes. And Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both companies, publicly warned earlier this month that AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade." He argued AI systems could gain sweeping power over the physical world and become capable of improving themselves without human input.
Some industry leaders, including executives at Anthropic and OpenAI, have called for a slowdown in AI development to better manage the risk. But other figures, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang, have argued some of the warnings are overblown.
Huang said Tuesday that "there's no conflict between innovation, technology and safety," arguing that tech companies are developing stronger AI safety technology as they improve AI's capabilities.
Mr. Trump has not backed stricter AI regulations, instead favoring voluntary safety reviews. He has frequently warned that a nationwide AI slowdown could dent the country's economy and give China's tech industry a chance to catch up.
The president told reporters Tuesday that AI will lead to "unbelievable growth for our country," and if bad actors seek to exploit it, "we're going to be able to nab them." He also said tech companies have an incentive to police themselves and each other because "their companies are at stake."
Beyond the safety worries, there are also mounting concerns about the impact that AI could have on the world — from the potential for large-scale job loss to the rapid development of data centers to support advanced AI models.
As more state and local governments push back on data center development, Mr. Trump said communities that accept the facilities will "greatly benefit financially."
"The data centers are making an absolute fortune. But now, the people are going to benefit directly, whether it's teachers that get paid a bonus, whether it's people that live in the community that get paid a dividend," he told CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes.
But lawmakers who favor more stringent AI regulations may be skeptical of voluntary standards set by the industry. In a statement shortly after Tuesday's meeting, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia called for Congress to pass mandatory testing, evaluation and incident reporting rules for the most advanced AI models.
"The companies building the most powerful AI systems are warning us that the technology is advancing faster than our safeguards," Warner said. "The president's response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves."

articles.title_orig: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.title_zh: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.content_orig:
Nine American citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in occupied West Bank since 2022
The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank , including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years.
The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children.
The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor.
Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee.
“While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.”
Nine Americans have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2022. The most recent include Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old from Tampa, Florida, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025 while visiting family in the village of Sinjil. His family said the settlers surrounded him for more than three hours and blocked an ambulance from reaching him as he tried to protect their land. Weeks later, Khamis Ayyad, a 40-year-old father of five from Cicero, Illinois, died of smoke inhalation after settlers set fire to cars and homes in the village of Silwad.
Two other Americans, both 17, Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Khdour, were shot dead in separate incidents in early 2024. Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old raised in Seattle, was shot in the head by Israeli troops, and Amer Rabee, a 14-year-old from New Jersey, was shot 11 times, according to Van Hollen.
The victim list also includes the journalist Shireen Abu Akleh , killed in 2022, and Omar Assad, an elderly man who died after Israeli soldiers bound and gagged him.
Van Hollen said none of the cases has ended in accountability, from either the Israeli or US government, and he places the blame largely on Republican senators who continue to vote against it.
“If the killing of nine Americans does not justify a report from our own state department, I would ask my colleagues: what would?” the Maryland Democrat said in a floor speech. “How many more Americans must be killed before the executive branch does its job? These families deserve answers.”
In August, 45 Democratic senators signed a letter to Benjamin Netanyahu urging him to act to protect Americans in the West Bank.
The vote comes amid what human rights groups describe as rising settler violence. Human Rights Watch in August reported that settler attacks, together with a rapid expansion of settlements, had fully or partly displaced 107 Palestinian communities, about 5,900 people, since January 2023. The group cited UN figures showing more Palestinians were displaced in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025.
A UN report from March covering the 12 months up to October 2025 documented 1,732 settler attacks causing injuries or property damage, and determined that Israel’s settlement expansion had forced more than 36,000 Palestinians from their homes.
Many of the Democrats , who have historically been in lockstep with Israel, have now shifted over the last few years.
When Sanders first forced a Senate vote on blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, 18 senators backed him. Then, in April of this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a $295m sale of bulldozers to Israel, which Sanders argued would be used to demolish homes in the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon. Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000lb bombs.
The measures failed because every Republican voted against them.

articles.title_orig: California bans officers’ use of electric-shock gloves after ICE reveals plan to equip agents
articles.title_zh: California bans officers’ use of electric-shock gloves after ICE reveals plan to equip agents
articles.content_orig:
State passes law banning local, state and federal officers from using gloves that deliver painful electric shocks
California has passed a law Tuesday banning local, state and federal law enforcement officers from using gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to people .
The ban on shock gloves will take effect next year and remain in place until 2030. It comes weeks after US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) moved to equip its officers with the gloves, which are designed to gain compliance from combative individuals. Last month, the agency awarded a nearly $17m contract to buy 6,000 pairs.
“Trump has put his political interests above the health, safety and livelihood of American families,” Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, said in a statement after signing the law. “California is taking action to strengthen transparency, accountability, and oversight around immigration enforcement in our state.”
The law is the latest example of how Democratic-led states have been pushing back against Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts since he took office last year. In California, lawmakers passed at least two dozen bills this year seeking to fortify immigrants’ rights, restrict cooperation with federal immigration agents and tighten regulations on immigrant detention facilities, among other things.
Nationwide, 17 states with Democratic-led legislatures have passed a total of more than 100 pro-immigrant bills this year, according to an Associated Press analysis using the bill tracking software Plural. The most common purpose is to limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement agents.
LaShae Sharp-Collins, a Democratic California assembly member, said she introduced the shock-gloves legislation to “put a pause” on law enforcement’s use of the devices while the state examines their potential risks. The law requires the state’s justice department to study their safety and report to lawmakers by 2029.
“There’s a lot of unrest and a lot of uncertainty,” she said in an interview. “A lot of people are scared.”
The law will again test the state’s authority to restrict federal agents amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. A federal judge earlier this year blocked the state’s first-in-the-nation law barring federal officers from wearing face coverings, deeming it too selective because it applied to local and federal law enforcement but exempted state officers.
Lawmakers passed a new bill this year to make the ban apply to all officers. Newsom signed that legislation.
Kevin Johnson, a professor emeritus at the University of California, Davis School of Law, said courts are likely to ultimately rule that the state cannot bar federal officers from wearing shock gloves or face coverings. The laws are well-intentioned, he said, but likely conflict with the supremacy clause of the US constitution, which generally sets federal law as supreme over conflicting state law.
“The state has very limited, if any, powers in dictating to the federal government how its officers are armed,” he said.
Sacramento sheriff Jim Cooper, a Democrat and former state lawmaker, said banning shock gloves “really makes no sense” because they are among the non-lethal tools officers can use if necessary.
“When the federal government does something, the state legislature wants to ban it,” he said at a news conference. “They’re making our job harder.”
Sharp-Collins said ICE’s plan to use shock gloves was the catalyst for the ban. But she cited their use by other officers, including a case in which a Kentucky family alleged a man died after being tased and shocked with the gloves dozens of times while in law enforcement custody in 2024.
Scott Wiener, a state senator and San Francisco Democrat who wrote last year’s mask ban, also authored this year’s measure to expand it to state officers.
“California must use every available tool to stand up for our communities under attack from ICE’s secret police terror campaign,” he said in a statement after it passed the legislature.

articles.title_orig: People with Type 2 diabetes lost up to 60 pounds on Lilly’s latest weight loss drug
articles.title_zh: People with Type 2 diabetes lost up to 60 pounds on Lilly’s latest weight loss drug
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Tennessee execution of lone woman on death row halted by federal appeals court
Eli Lilly’s highly anticipated GLP-1 drug retatrutide helped people with Type 2 diabetes lose up to 60 pounds, or about 23% of their body weight, according to late-stage trial results published Tuesday in The Lancet.
It’s the most weight loss ever recorded in a drug trial for diabetes patients, a group that often has a harder time losing weight.
In clinical trials for semaglutide and tirzepatide , people with Type 2 diabetes lost up to 10% (21 pounds) and 15% (34 pounds) of their body weight, respectively. (Those are not direct comparisons, as the drugs were not evaluated in head-to-head clinical trials.)
Retatrutide “is truly an advance in diabetes care,” said Dr. Susan Spratt, an endocrinologist and the senior medical director for the Population Health Management Office at Duke Health in North Carolina. She was not involved in the trial and does not receive money from Eli Lilly. “It rivals gastric bypass surgery without the surgery.”
Spratt said many diabetes medications, such as insulin, cause weight gain.
“It can be discouraging to manage your diabetes well but gain weight,” she said.
Lilly’s trial included more than 1,110 patients who had an average starting weight of about 234 pounds and an average body mass index, or BMI, of about 38. People were randomly assigned to take one of three weekly doses of retatrutide or a placebo for 80 weeks. By the end of the trial, more than half of participants’ BMI fell below 30, the cutoff for obesity.
Results from another trial, published Tuesday in the New England Journal of Medicine , found retatrutide helped patients without Type 2 diabetes who have obesity or are overweight lose up to 70 pounds, or 25% of their body weight on average, after 80 weeks. That data included a subset of patients with severe obesity, who lost up to 85 pounds, or 30% of their body weight, after 104 weeks — the most weight loss ever recorded in a medication trial and on par with bariatric surgery.
Like semaglutide and tirzepatide, retatrutide works by mimicking a hormone called GLP-1. What sets retatrutide apart is its classification as a “triple agonist.” Lilly’s tirzepatide, a “double agonist,” mimics two hormones (GLP-1 and GIP), and retatrutide targets three by adding a hormone called glucagon.
Lilly hasn’t submitted retatrutide for approval to the Food and Drug Administration, but its clinical trial results have already cemented it as one of the drug industry’s most highly anticipated treatments. Lilly says it plans to file for approval early next year.
Unauthorized, copycat versions of retatrutide are already being made and sold through wellness platforms, med spas and compounding pharmacies. The drug is often labeled as “for research use only,” a legal workaround to sell compounds they claim aren’t meant for humans. Lilly has filed lawsuits against companies selling unapproved versions of the drug.
Retatrutide also helps reduce the severity of sleep apnea and lower knee arthritis pain. Earlier data suggests the drug appears to help the heart.
The new trial found that retatrutide, like other GLP-1 drugs, which were initially developed as diabetes medications, effectively lowered blood sugar levels in patients with diabetes.
Retatrutide lowered A1C levels — a measure of a person’s average blood sugar levels over the previous two to three months — by up to 1.6%, compared with 0.2% with a placebo, according to the trial results.
Up to 40% of patients in the trial reached an A1C below 5.7%, below the cutoff for diabetes and prediabetes.
“The retatrutide data is very exciting,” Dr. Michelle Ponder, an assistant professor of medicine at Duke University School of Medicine in North Carolina, wrote in an email. A 5.7% A1C level means “that their diabetes went into remission,” said Ponder, who was not involved with Lilly’s trial.
She added, however, that retatrutide “may be too strong for some patients,” particularly those with only mild diabetes or slightly elevated weight.
They “may be better suited to the medications we already have available on the market such as Ozempic or Mounjaro,” she said.
She added that whenever switching medications, there is a chance patients could experience a change in the frequency of side effects.
Side effects of retatrutide were similar to those of other GLP-1 medications, with patients most commonly reporting diarrhea, nausea, constipation and vomiting. Lilly said the side effects were mild to moderate in severity. About 8% of people in the trial taking the highest dose stopped taking the drug, compared with about 5% of people taking the placebo.
Berkeley Lovelace Jr. is a health and medical reporter for NBC News. He covers the Food and Drug Administration, with a special focus on Covid vaccines, prescription drug pricing and health care. He previously covered the biotech and pharmaceutical industry with CNBC.

articles.title_orig: 'Digger' Confronts Negative Reviews: New Ad Defends Tom Cruise Movie
articles.title_zh: 'Digger' Confronts Negative Reviews: New Ad Defends Tom Cruise Movie
articles.content_orig:
Warner Bros. is asking moviegoers to “decide for yourself” with a new ad for Tom Cruise’s “ Digger ” that touts both negative and positive reactions.
“Masterpiece” and “Unpleasant” are quoted in the same still of the new trailer, which also toggles between the words “Brilliant” and “Baffling” as well as “Magnificent” and “Insufferable.” These quotes are from film influencers who screened the movie early and posted their reactions after the social embargo lifted on Sept. 22.
“Same film, different truth,” reads the ad for “Digger,” which stars Cruise as an oil tycoon whose drilling triggers a climate crisis. The film, from director Alejandro G. Iñárritu, marks Cruise’s first non-action hero role in nearly a decade.
Warner Bros. posted the new ad an hour before the review embargo, which is when film critics were allowed to publish their reviews. The “decide for yourself” campaign may have been an attempt to get ahead of the critics, who were, as a whole, far less generous than the first wave of social media pundits.
Variety ‘s Owen Gleiberman called the film “so full of itself” in his review , writing, “The movie cost north of $125 million to make, and that figure is not only too big to probably justify itself; it’s a testament to the arrogance of the filmmakers — to the assumption that we’ll turn out in droves for this ponderous absurdist lecture.”
Bilge Ebiri of Vulture wrote in his review, “‘Digger’ is a torturous experience, sometimes purposefully so, often unintentionally so.” And David Ehrlich of IndieWire dubbed it a “surreal misfire,” giving the movie a C+ grade. (“Digger” currently sits at a 52% score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes.)
Of course, those are just critics’ opinions, so for those waiting to decide for themselves, “Digger” premieres in theaters on Oct. 2.
